summary.text: Intermolecular forces are the attractions and repulsions between neighbouring particles, such as atoms, molecules and ions, where no ionic, covalent or metallic bond forms.
They are weak next to the forces that hold a molecule together: a covalent bond, built on shared electron pairs, is much stronger than the pull between neighbouring molecules.
They matter most in biochemistry, because every enzymatic reaction begins with an interaction between the substrate and the enzyme.

items.prompt: A student compares the grip holding two atoms together inside one molecule with the pull between that molecule and its neighbour. How do the two compare?

options.label: The pull between molecules is stronger, since it acts over more atoms
Both are about equally strong, since both are electrical attractions
The grip inside the molecule is much stronger than the outside pull
The outside pull is stronger only when the molecules are polar

items.explain: Intermolecular forces are weak relative to the forces holding a molecule together; a covalent bond is much stronger than the forces between neighbouring molecules.

items.prompt: Two neighbouring particles attract each other, yet no new chemical bond forms between them. What would chemists call this pull?

options.label: An intermolecular force between the two particles
An ionic bond that happens to be very weak
A metallic bond that forms only at short range
An intramolecular force that holds one molecule together

items.explain: Interactions between particles where ionic, covalent or metallic bonds do not form count as intermolecular forces.

items.prompt: A biochemist asks why weak attractions between molecules matter so much in biochemistry. What is the best reason?

options.label: They make covalent bonds form more quickly inside molecules
They are what hold the atoms of each molecule together
They keep molecules from ever coming into contact
Each reaction driven by an enzyme starts with such an interaction

items.explain: All enzymatic reactions begin with intermolecular interactions between the substrate and the enzyme, which is why they matter so much in biochemistry.

items.prompt: Carbon dioxide contains polar groups of atoms, yet the molecule as a whole has no net dipole moment. What explains this?

options.label: Its atoms are too far apart to carry any partial charge
Its symmetry makes the individual pulls cancel each other out
Its carbon atom carries a full charge that hides the others
Its electrons are shared equally by every atom nearby

items.explain: Symmetry within the molecule makes the dipoles of its groups cancel, as in tetrachloromethane and carbon dioxide.

items.prompt: A charged particle sits near a polar molecule, while two polar molecules sit near each other. Which attraction is stronger?

options.label: The first pair, since the charged particle carries much more charge
The second pair, since two polar molecules offer twice as many ends
Neither; they pull equally since both involve a polar molecule
The second pair, since uncharged molecules attract more evenly

items.explain: Ion–dipole forces are stronger than dipole–dipole interactions because an ion's charge is much greater than the charge of a dipole moment.

items.prompt: Water boils at 100 °C, higher than the other group 16 hydrides. Which explanation fits?

options.label: Water molecules are much heavier than the other hydrides
Water has stronger covalent bonds, so it takes more heat to boil
Water molecules cling to each other by hydrogen bonding, which the others barely manage
Water molecules carry a full ionic charge, unlike the others

items.explain: Intermolecular hydrogen bonding is responsible for water's high boiling point compared with the other group 16 hydrides, which have little capability to hydrogen bond.

beats.title: The weak pulls between molecules
beats.hook: Atoms are locked together firmly inside a molecule, yet the pulls reaching between molecules are far weaker.

beats.prompt: Two molecules sit side by side. Compared with the covalent bond that joins atoms inside each molecule, how strong is the pull between the two molecules?

right.label: A hydrogen on nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine, drawn to another electronegative atom

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning about attraction strengths is wrong. Which?

steps.text: An ion's charge is much greater than the charge of a dipole moment.
So ion–dipole forces are stronger than dipole–dipole interactions.
Ion–dipole bonding is weaker than hydrogen bonding.
So a hydrogen bond is a stronger pull than an ion–dipole force.

beats.explain: Ion–dipole bonding is stronger than hydrogen bonding, so the third step reverses the ranking.

beats.idea: Intermolecular forces are attractions between neighbouring particles that are much weaker than the covalent bonds inside a molecule.

paragraphs.heading: What they are
paragraphs.text: An intermolecular force is a push or pull between neighbouring particles, such as atoms, molecules or ions. It includes the electromagnetic attraction and repulsion acting between them. In the widest sense, it is any interaction between particles in which no chemical bond forms, whether ionic, covalent or metallic. These forces are weak next to the forces inside a molecule. A covalent bond, where atoms share pairs of electrons, is much stronger than the pull between molecules sitting side by side.

paragraphs.heading: Why they matter
paragraphs.text: Intermolecular interactions are much weaker than covalent ones, and they do not greatly rearrange the electrons of the particles involved. Even so, they are especially important in biochemistry and molecular biology. Every reaction carried out by an enzyme begins with an intermolecular interaction between the enzyme and its substrate. These interactions are the basis of enzymology.

paragraphs.heading: How they are studied
paragraphs.text: Scientists learn about these forces by measuring properties of bulk matter, such as viscosity, pressure, volume and temperature. Mathematical tools called virial coefficients and pair potentials, such as the Lennard-Jones potential, connect those measurements to the microscopic picture. The earliest known reference to the nature of microscopic forces comes from Alexis Clairaut, in a book published in Paris in 1743. Laplace, Gauss, Maxwell, Boltzmann and Pauling later added to the work.

paragraphs.heading: Hydrogen bonds
paragraphs.text: A hydrogen bond is an attraction between a hydrogen atom covalently joined to a highly electronegative element, usually nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine, and a second atom that is also highly electronegative. It is often described as a strong electrostatic interaction. Yet it also behaves partly like a covalent bond: it points in a set direction and is stronger than a van der Waals interaction. Hydrogen bonds between water molecules give water its high boiling point of 100 °C, compared with the other hydrides of group 16, which can hardly form such bonds.

paragraphs.heading: Dipoles pulling on dipoles
paragraphs.text: Some molecules have a permanent dipole: one end carries a partial positive charge and the other a partial negative charge. Dipole–dipole forces, also called Keesom interactions, are the electrostatic attractions between such molecules. In hydrogen chloride, HCl, the positive end of one molecule pulls on the negative end of the next and shifts its position. This force is stronger than London forces but weaker than the pull between two ions, since only partial charges take part. Molecules such as carbon dioxide and tetrachloromethane contain dipolar groups, but their symmetry makes the dipoles cancel, leaving the molecule as a whole with no dipole.

paragraphs.heading: When ions join in
paragraphs.text: When a positive site attracts a negative site, chemists call it ion pairing or a salt bridge, and it comes mainly from electrostatic forces. An ion next to a polar molecule gives an ion–dipole force, with the two lining up so that positive and negative groups sit side by side for the greatest pull. This is stronger than a dipole–dipole force, since an ion carries far more charge than a dipole does. It is also stronger than hydrogen bonding.
